forWhom.headline: Three moments when processes break faster than org charts can fix them.
forWhom.lead: Makigami works for any admin process. VSM works for any company producing goods. These tools are universal — but three trigger situations burn the loudest right now.

reshoring.title: The AI Mandate
reshoring.body: Leadership wants AI in every process by next quarter. But a model can only automate what's been mapped — point it at a chaotic process and you scale the chaos, not the output. Map the flow first, then automate the part that's actually ready.

surge.title: The Demand Surge
surge.body: Pharma, defense, medtech, energy — demand just doubled. Capacity didn't. Overtime masks the waste; mapping the flow shows where hours actually disappear so you add throughput, not headcount.

outgrown.title: The Outgrown Process
outgrown.body: You grew by patching. Ten years of workarounds, three ERP migrations, four re-orgs — and nobody can draw the current state end-to-end. Before the next change, make the chaos visible.

forWhom.consultantStrip: Consultants & Lean coaches: run LeanTheCompany across your whole client book — multi-workspace, white-label A3s, revenue share on referred seats.

problem.headline: You don't have a people problem. You have an invisibility problem.
problem.quote: "Where there is no standard, there can be no kaizen." — Taiichi Ohno
problem.lead: Every factory and every office runs on three kinds of waste that nobody writes down because nobody can see them. Until you draw them.

chaos.label: 01 · Chaos
chaos.title: Nobody knows the real process.
chaos.body: Ask five people to map the order-to-ship flow and you’ll get five different versions. The current-state map on the wall is three years old and two ERP migrations out of date. You’re making decisions based on a process that no longer exists — and nobody can explain why the complaint rate isn’t improving, or even agree on what “good enough” looks like.

handoffs.title: Handoffs eat more time than the work.
handoffs.label: 02 · Handoffs
handoffs.body: The machine cycle is 40 seconds. The order spends 11 days between people, inboxes and "waiting for clarification." Speed lives in the white space, not the value-added steps.

shadow.label: 03 · Shadow
shadow.title: Half the work isn't in any system.
shadow.body: Senior operators and admins run parallel spreadsheets, side-channel chats and heroic workarounds. When they leave, the knowledge leaves. When they stay, the knowledge never scales.

howItConnects.headline: Most tools start with the map. We start with the promise.

steps.title: Define what you promised.
steps.body: Choose your industry — the five things your customers judge you on are already there.

steps.title: Grade yourself, 1 to 5.
steps.body: Current against target, with defined criteria at every level. Evidence, not a show of hands.

steps.title: Put a number on every gap.
steps.body: Which measure proves it, how large the loss is, how much you trust the data. Now you know where to look — before you draw anything.

steps.title: Map where the loss lives.
steps.body: The flow the loss sits in decides the map.

steps.title: Fix it, and keep it fixed.
steps.body: Improvement work with an owner and a due date — then the one page your management review actually reads.

sensei.body: Not a step — it runs the length of the line. Ask where your biggest waste is at any point, and the answer comes from your takt, your handoffs, your losses.

howItConnects.closing: Direction first. Then the map. Then the improvement. Never the other way round.

diagnostic.headline: Measure your process chaos in 5 questions.
diagnostic.lead: Five questions about how work actually moves through your plant. The score lands on the screen when you finish — no email, no waiting. Each answer comes back with the note I'd give you standing on the line next to you.

inventory.title: Inventory between steps
inventory.ask: How much of an order’s lead time is waiting versus actual processing time?
options: Work keeps moving.
A day or two of waiting for a few hours of work.
Several days of waiting. I don’t really know how much of that time is actual work.
I don’t know — we’ve never measured the waiting time against the actual work time.

handoffs.title: Handoffs per order
handoffs.ask: How many different people or systems touch an order from quote to shipment?
options: Fewer than five, and I know exactly who or what they are.
Five to ten.
More than ten.
Nobody has ever drawn it end to end.

shadow.title: Shadow spreadsheets
shadow.ask: How many critical Excel files live on personal drives instead of systems of record?
options: None that I know of.
One or two, with clear ownership.
Several, and at least one is critical to the operation.
The plant would struggle to operate without them.

decisions.title: Decision cycle time
decisions.ask: When a problem surfaces on the shop floor, how long does it take to reach someone with the authority to make a decision?
options: Within the shift.
A day or two.
The decision waits for the weekly meeting.
It depends entirely on who is available.

standards.title: Standardised work
standards.ask: What percentage of your key operations have a one-page standard that is understood and followed by everyone?
options: Most of them, and the standards are kept up to date.
About half — and some of those standards are out of date.
Only a few — and most were created for audit compliance rather than daily use.
Almost none. Everyone works to their own method.

firefighting.name: Firefighting
firefighting.line: Your problem isn’t capacity. It’s visibility.

runningOnPeople.name: Dependent on People
runningOnPeople.line: The process works because specific people keep it running. That’s not a system — it’s dependency disguised as one.

drifting.name: Drifting
drifting.line: Nothing is on fire. But several problems are smouldering beneath the surface, and their effects compound over time.

quietPlant.name: Quiet plant
quietPlant.line: Rare. Either the process is genuinely under control, or nobody has looked closely enough yet.

diagnostic.introBody: Answer from the reality on the floor, not from what the report says. Your results stay private unless you choose to share them.

space.headline: One Space, one process, seen properly.
space.p1: An Operational Space is one business process — mapped as it actually runs today, and as it should run instead.
space.p2: You map the office flow with a Makigami and the material flow with a value stream map. You mark where the time really goes. Then you draw the future state, and the kaizen cards are the work that gets you from one to the other.
space.p3: One Space holds all of it, including the record of what you tried and what happened. Add another Space for the next process. That is the whole system.

archive.headline: A Space doesn't get abandoned. It graduates.
archive.p1: Your plan sets how many Spaces you can work in at once. It does not set how many you can keep.
archive.p2: When a process is good enough and stable enough to run without you, that Space is finished — so you archive it. It stays readable, printable, exportable, and it never counts against your active limit again. Bring it back whenever you want. Nothing is ever deleted.
archive.p3: Keep everything you finish. And if you stop subscribing, you keep read-only access to all of it for two years, with export available the whole time. We’ll remind you before anything goes.
archive.p4: You did the work. It’s yours.

comparison.headline: You could do this on a whiteboard. People try.
comparison.p1: Miro, Lucidchart, a PowerPoint template — €5 to €9 a month for shapes and arrows. They're good tools. They just don't know anything.
comparison.p2: A blank canvas doesn't know what a value stream is. It won't tell you your Makigami has a handoff loop in it, it won't turn the map into an A3 your steering group will actually read, and it won't still be there in eleven months when the consultant has gone and nobody remembers why the board was drawn that way. And when you stop paying for one of those, your boards go read-only and you're told to delete some to get back in. We don't do that. Archive what you finish, keep it forever, and if you leave you still have two years and an export button.
comparison.p3: That's the difference. Not the canvas — what the canvas knows, and whether it's still yours.

about.headline: Three industries. The same problem keeps surfacing. That’s why LeanTheCompany exists.
about.title: Founder · Sensei
about.tagline: Engineer, operator, coach. 25+ years across Europe and Asia — from the shop floor to the boardroom — before I wrote a single line of code.
about.lead: My career in operations management began at Tetra Pak. Ten years of hands-on experience on the production line gave me a solid foundation in manufacturing, operations and continuous improvement, and shaped the working methods I still use today: seeing the actual workflow, understanding the real problems that arise on site and the gap between process design and actual operation.
bio: Companies change. Products change. Operating environments change. Yet the underlying process problems are often remarkably similar. Years of practice reinforced a simple principle: consultants can help solve individual problems, but sustainable improvement depends on an organization’s ability to see how work actually flows, identify the gaps between current and target performance, and improve the system continuously.

That is why I created LeanTheCompany — a management system shaped by more than two decades of operational practice, tested and refined across different industries and operating environments. It gives teams a structured way to see the process, set improvement priorities, and turn improvement into an internal capability — not an external dependency.
